name: Zaar
catalog_citation: Caron, Bernard. 2013 (v3 2015). Zaar Grammatical Sketch. LLACAN (Inalco, CNRS). HAL halshs-00647526. Phonology section stated to be based on Schneeberg (1974) Sayanci Phonology.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.3 'Tone system' (p. 5-6); sec. 6 verb tone classes (p. 11); sec. 18 'Intonation' (p. 32); whole document searched: 0 occurrences of 'stress'
catalog_quote: Zaar has a three-tier tone system: H (marked with an acute accent: á), M (unmarked: a), L (marked with a grave accent: à). Initial nonimplosive voiced obstruents have a depressor effect on tones in a some grammatical environments ... L tone tends to spread over M clitics (tonal sandhi). ... Zaar has two verb tone classes: Middle (M) and High (H), which can be contrasted in the Perfective. ... The role of pitch in Zaar intonation can be observed in the variation between lexical and grammatical tones as they are perceived and transcribed by the native speaker and their acoustic realization.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the held Caron sketch at the stated sections/pages; two further held Caron primaries (2005 dictionary-grammar, 2015 Tone and Intonation) and two newly fetched sources Caron intonation papers all describe Zaar as a three-tone language (H/M/L + F/R contours, depressor consonants, grammatical tone) with no word-stress or accent rule, and the 2015 Benjamins chapter explicitly contrasts Zaar's 'tone system' with lexical-stress and pitch-accent systems elsewhere in Afroasiatic. Caron is the principal describer; no reference grammar exists per Glottolog. The one unheld higher-type source, Schneeberg 1974 Sayanci Phonology (diss.), is the basis Caron cites and is unlikely to overturn a 'tonal, no stress rule described' coding; listed as a medium-priority wishlist item only. web lookups quota was exhausted, so the web sweep was limited to the HAL API (32 Caron Zaar records, none

The intonation of Topic and Focus: Zaar (Nigeria), Tamasheq (Niger), Juba Arabic (South Sudan) and Tripoli Arabic (Libya). In A. Mettouchi, M. Vanhove & D. Caubet (eds.), Corpus-based Studies of Lesser-described Languages: The CorpAfroAs corpus of spoken AfroAsiatic languages (Studies in Corpus Linguistics 68), 63-115. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. HAL halshs-00922747.
sources.quote: 'Afroasiatic languages have phonologized pitch into different prosodic systems that vary from a demarcative accent system, e.g. Berber; to a lexical stress system, e.g. Tripoli Arabic; a pitch accent system, e.g. Juba Arabic; and a tone system, e.g. Hausa and Zaar' (p. 2); 'Zaar is a tone language with three phonemic tones: High ... Mid ... Low. Two contour tones result from the combinations High-Mid and Low-Mid on a single syllable' (p. 5); 'There is no intensity stress on the focus' (p. 10).
